titleStmt.title: SIRAJ: Diverse and Efficient Red-Teaming for LLM Agents via Distilled Structured Reasoning

analytic.title: SIRAJ: Diverse and Efficient Red-Teaming for LLM Agents via Distilled Structured Reasoning

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The ability of LLM agents to plan and invoke tools exposes them to new safety risks, making a comprehensive red-teaming system crucial for discovering vulnerabilities and ensuring their safe deployment. We present SIRAJ: a generic red-teaming framework for arbitrary black-box LLM agents. We employ a dynamic two-step process that starts with an agent definition and generates diverse seed test cases that cover various risk outcomes, tool-use trajectories, and risk sources. Then, it iteratively constructs and refines model-based adversarial attacks based on the execution trajectories of former attempts. To optimize the red-teaming cost, we present a model distillation approach that leverages structured forms of a teacher model's reasoning to train smaller models that are equally effective. Across diverse evaluation agent settings, our seed test case generation approach yields 2 -2.5x boost to the coverage of risk outcomes and tool-calling trajectories. Our distilled 8B red-teamer model improves attack success rate by 100%, surpassing the 671B Deepseek-R1 model. Our ablations and analyses validate the effectiveness of the iterative framework, structured reasoning, and the generalization of our red-teamer models.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The growing deployment of Large Language Model (LLM) agents, which leverage planning and tool use to accomplish complex tasks (Yao et al., 2023;Deng et al., 2023;Qin et al., 2023), has introduced significant safety concerns. Being able to perform unethical actions in the real world, such agents can cause more severe and diverse harm than traditional LLMs (Debenedetti et al., 2024;Zhan et al., 2024;Zhang et al., 2024b;Andriushchenko et al., 2024;Yang et al., 2025b;Vijayvargiya et al., 2025). Therefore, a critical step before deploying LLM * Work done during Kaiwen Zhou's internship at Microsoft. agents in real-world applications is to conduct comprehensive safety evaluation and red-teaming for them to uncover any potential risks they might introduce. However, existing agent safety evaluations lack the necessary diversity, covering only coarsegrained safety categories without considering finegrained risks for a given agent (Zhang et al., 2024b;Andriushchenko et al., 2024;Yang et al., 2025b;Vijayvargiya et al., 2025). Furthermore, existing agents red-teaming frameworks are limited, either require impractical white-box access to the agent or target a narrow class of risks (Xu et al., 2024;Zhang et al., 2025;Wang et al., 2025), which is insufficient for the diverse and complex threats that agents may encounter.

To address these gaps, we propose SIRAJ:foot_0 a unified framework for agents red-teaming that only requires a black-box access to the agents under evaluation. First, to ensure diverse coverage, we focus on fine-grained risk outcomes within broader safety categories. For example, for the risk category "leak private / sensitive information", we consider various types of private information, such as user credentials, personal data, etc. Moreover, as each fine-grained risk can be triggered in multiple ways, we consider different ways that an agent can lead to each risk, which we represent by the action sequence (trajectory) that the agent takes as well as the risk source (a malicious user vs. a malicious environment) that lead to each risk e.g., an agent can leak a password when the user directly asks for it, or when the agent is compromised by a malicious website.

Secondly, we propose a model-based redteaming framework that iteratively generates adversarial test cases with red-teaming strategies, based on the agent's execution trajectories of previous attempts. However, applying such methods with large models is costly and time-consuming. Therefore, we introduce the structured reasoning distillation approach to train a significantly smaller redteamer models. We first propose a structured reasoning format for red-teaming that decomposes the reasoning process into distinct components. Then, we collect successful red-teaming attempts from a large teacher model that is prompted to follow our structured reasoning format, which are then used to train a smaller student model via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL) to further improve its red-teaming effectiveness.

Our experiments show that the proposed seed test case generation significantly improves the evaluation diversity over baselines, achieving around 2x greater tool-calling trajectory diversity and 2.5x risk outcome diversity. Furthermore, our redteamer distillation improves the attack success rate of Qwen3-8B by over 100%, surpasing that of Deepseek-R1 (671B). Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our iterative framework, structured reasoning, and both the SFT and RL training stages, showing that our red-teamer generalizes to novel agent settings and risk types.

Our contributions include: 1) A two-step seed test case generation method that dynamically generates safety test cases for arbitrary agents with high diversity in risk outcomes, tool-calling trajectories, and risk sources; 2) A fully black-box adversarial red-teaming method that can target diverse risks of LLM agents. Our method employs iterative adversarial refinement with the execution trajectories as feedback; 3) A novel method for reasoning model distillation in which we replace long and repetitive raw reasoning traces with concise structured forms before the distillation process; 4) Extensive experiments and ablations that demonstrate the effectiveness of each component of our framework in generating diverse test cases and adversarially attacking various LLM agents.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: LLM Agents Safety Evaluation and Automatic Red-teaming With the increasing deployment of LLM agents in real-world applications, ensuring their safety and reliability has become a critical concern. Recent works have explored various aspects of LLM agents safety evaluation, including safety benchmarks on user-harmful instructions (Andriushchenko et al., 2024), environment-based harms such as prompt injection (Zhan et al., 2024;Debenedetti et al., 2024), web pop-ups (Zhang et al., 2024a), and the combinations of them (Yang et al., 2025b;Zhang et al., 2024b;Vijayvargiya et al., 2025;Tur et al., 2025;Ma, 2025). Moreover, recent works have also investigated adversarial redteaming to further uncover potential vulnerabilities in LLM agents (Chen et al., 2024;Xu et al., 2024;Zhang et al., 2025;Wang et al., 2025). Ad-vAgent (Xu et al., 2024) proposes to use supervised fine-tuning and DPO to train a red-teaming LLM that can generate adversarial prompt injections, but it shows weak generalization to different LLMs. AgentVigil (Wang et al., 2025) also proposes a multi-round mutation strategy to generate adversarial prompt injections. UDora (Zhang et al., 2025) proposes an optimization-based string insertion approach to attack LLM agents, requiring a white-box access to the underlying model. On the contrary, our approach only requires a black-box access to the evaluated agents which makes it widely applicable. Furthermore, we explicitly optimize for the diversity of the evaluation without making any assumptions about the target agents.

LLM Red-teaming Red-teaming LLMs has been an active research topic. Jailbreak attacks have been widely studied to bypass the safety guardrails of LLMs, including string-based attacks (Zou et al., 2023) and strategy-based attacks (Liu et al., 2024;Zhou et al., 2025). Among the strategybased attacks, recent works have explored finetuning a red-teamer LLM to generate more effective adversarial strategies and prompts (Ge et al., 2023;Beutel et al., 2024;Liu et al., 2025;Guo et al., 2025b). Besides improving attack success, recent works have also discussed the importance of diversity in red-teaming (Samvelyan et al., 2024;Beutel et al., 2024). This includes the coverage of different attack styles/strategies and the coverage of different safety categories. Our work is the first to discuss and study the problem of comprehensive red-teaming for LLM agents. We achieve diversity on several angles with a two-step seed test case generation process. Our iterative adversarial transformation approach retains effective red-teaming results (i.e., high attack success rate) while being cost-efficient.

div.head: Preliminaries
div.p: Definitions An LLM agent A is an arbitrary backbone LLM paired with a set of tools U that it can call (e.g., send emails, web search). To execute an input task (e.g., "Send me an email with last week's Champions League updates"), A follows a sequence of tool calls, which we refer to as a trajectory H. Our safety evaluation starts with a target risk category, e.g., "Leak private information", which spans diverse potential fine-grained risk outcomes (e.g., "Leak a password"), each of which can be triggered by the task instruction (e.g., an adversarial user) or a malicious environment. We refer to the trigger as the risk source.

div.head: Diverse and Efficient Automatic Red-Teaming
div.p: We consider the following task: Given an LLM agent A and a set of target risk categories C, test and uncover as many potential fine-grained risk outcomes within each category that A is susceptible to as possible. A risk outcome can be triggered in various ways (agent trajectories), e.g., leaking bank account information can happen when the agent is asked to send an email, or make a post on social media. Likewise, a risk can be triggered by the user task or the environment. Hence, we expand the diversity goal of the red-teaming to further include both execution trajectories and risk source. We assume only a black-box access to A and its backbone model, i.e., only execution trajectories and model outputs are accessible during the automatic red-teaming process. The effectiveness of the red-teaming process is measured in terms of the attack success rate (ASR) of the test cases, which is the ratio of test cases that yield a risky outcome. A key aspect that we consider is the efficiency of the red-teaming process. We aim to retain the effectiveness of the red-teaming process with significantly reduced compute.

Framework overview We explicitly disentangle the diversity and the adversarial nature of the evaluation in a two-step framework (Figure 1) that synthesizes risky tasks in the first step and transforms them into adversarial variants in the second step. Given target risk categories C and an agent definition A, we generate seed test cases T while ensuring coverage of fine-grained risk outcomes, risk sources, and execution trajectories (Section 4). Then, the second step iteratively attempts to generate adversarial test cases T ′ that successfully yield the pre-determined fine-grained risk outcomes, source and trajectory in the first step (Section 5).

div.head: Seed Test Case Generation
div.p: To satisfy the diversity requirements, we propose a two-step seed test case generation process. The task is to generate a set of test cases T given the agent's available tools U and a set of safety categories C. First, for each safety category c ∈ C, we generate a set of risk outcomes R based on the agent's U. Then, we generates a set of test cases T for each risk outcome r ∈ R. Both steps are implemented with a prompt-based approach (Appendix A.10). Specifically, the test case generator takes as input the risk outcome r, the safety category c, the agent's tools U, and the formerly generated test cases for this risk outcome{t 1 , ...t i-1 }, and is prompted to generate a new test case t i that has a different trajectory or a different environment adversary conditions from the former test cases:
div.formula: t i = Test-Case-Generator(r, c, U, {t 1 , ...t i-1 })
div.p: (1) The test case t i includes a user instruction that describes the agent's task, the environment content that the agent needs to complete the task (e.g. the content of an email), the presence of an environment adversary e adv , and the anticipated execution trajectory H of the agent to achieve the risk outcome r. Here, including e adv and H in the test case helps the generation of novel test cases. In Section 6, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our two-step prompting approach compared to alternative variants.

div.head: Model-based Adversarial Red-Teaming
div.p: The risky intent in the seed test cases can be easily detectable by safety aligned LLM agent. This, however, does not mean that the agent is safe. In reality, the agent may face adversarial inputs introduced in its execution environment or by a malicious user.

To turn raw test cases into adversarial attacks, we take a model-based approach, following (Beutel et al., 2024;Liu et al., 2025). First we establish the effectiveness of reasoning models for the task.

Then, we propose an iterative prompting method for reasoning models that revises adversarial test cases based on agents' execution trajectories. To optimize the efficiency, we finally outline a method for distilling the red-teaming effectiveness of large reasoning models into smaller ones.

div.head: Reasoning Models as Red-Teamers
div.p: In Table 2, we use Qwen3-8B as an adversarial test case generation model. We compare both its reasoning and non-reasoning variants, and report ASRs on three agent models (details to follow in Section 6). The results clearly demonstrate the advantage of reasoning models, particularly in small models regime, for the agent red-teaming task. Hence, we adopt them for the adversarial generation step.

div.head: Iterative Adversarial Generation
div.p: We formulate adversarial test case generation as iteratively refining test cases until they successfully trigger the target risk. Each refinement step selects and applies a subset of red-teaming strategies S t to the seed test cases t (0) . We compile a library S lib of such strategies from previous work, including technical slang, authority manipulation, urgency, adding context, etc. (Full list in Appendix A.9) (Liu et al., 2025;Samvelyan et al., 2024;Liu et al., 2024;Zhou et al., 2025). We provide the red-teamer model with the execution trajectories H i-1 of the agent on former red-teaming attempts. As a result, the red-teamer can better think about the former test case execution and the reason of its failure to yield the target risk, and thus generate a more effective adversarial test case.
div.formula: S t , t (i) = Red-Teamer(t (0) , S lib , H i-1 ) (2)
div.p: Consistency Constraints We also need to ensure that the generated adversarial test cases do not change the original intent and semantics of the seed test case. To achieve this, we introduce a set of consistency constraints in our prompt (Appendix A.10) including preserving the risk category, risk outcome, the tool trajectory of the seed test case, as well as the intent of the instruction from the user or from the environment.

div.head: Red-Teamer Distillation via Structured Reasoning
div.p: With our iterative red-teaming framework, a large model, e.g., Deepseek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025a) can be significantly more effective than small models (Table 5). However, there are two challenges in directly applying such large reasoning models for adversarial generation task: (i) They are costly (due to their massive number of parameters) and slow, making them impractical for large-scale red-teaming.

(ii) The reasoning process of such models is typically verbose and repetitive, which not only affect their own attack effectiveness, but also makes it hard (Table 5) to distill them into smaller models for the red-teaming task. Therefore, we first introduce a structured reasoning format for agents

Structured Reasoning Understanding the test case: -goal: trigger risky behavior of clicking … -current user instruction: … Why the original test case and former red-team attempts failed: -The assistant detect and avoid leaking the information … What strategies to use now: -Urgency: Pressure the assistant to act … How to implement these strategies: -Instruction tweaks (Urgency + Emotional manipulation): …

div.head: Prompt
div.p: You are working as a red-team member to refine the safety test case… Here are the list of red-team strategies you can select to use: {redteam_strategies} Here is the test case you need to refine: {test_case} Here are the agent's execution trajectories for this test case, including results and used strategies from previous refinement rounds: ===== Round 1 ===== Agent: search_email() Env: "We detected unusual activity affecting …" Agent: ... This is a phishing message….

Unstructured Reasoning … In ROUND 2, the agent then performed the tool calls but still refused… We can modify the environment (the email content) to make it look more legitimate (e.g., by using …) Alternatively, we can also use strategies like … However, note that the agent's refusal in ROUND 2 was: … We need to convince the agent that … red-teaming to guide and compress the reasoning process, and then we distill large teacher models into smaller ones specifically for the adversarial red-teaming task. We employ both supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) for the distillation process.

Structured reasoning To address the verbose and arbitrary thinking process of large reasoning models (Deepseek-R1 in our setup, Figure . 2), we introduce a reasoning structure particularly for the iterative adversarial transformation task. Our proposed structure consists of 4 reasoning sections: (i) understanding the test case, (ii) analyzing why the original test case and former red-teaming attempts failed, (iii) thinking about what strategies to use, and (iv) practice how to implement these strategies. Prompting a large reasoning model to reason in this structure improves its effectiveness (Table 5). More importantly, we show that distilling large models into smaller models via that reasoning structure significantly improves the effectiveness of the distilled model compared to distilling the raw (unstructured) reasoning chain directly. We find that structured reasoning can reduce the noise in the reasoning process, resulting in higher quality SFT data. A full example of the processed structured reasoning is shown in Table 10 in the Appendix A.6.

SFT data collection. We synthesize 200 "training agents", each with a unique combination of 2-4 toolkits sampled by GPT-5 from the toolkits introduced in Agent-SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024b). Then, we prompt GPT-5 using our seed test case generation method (Section 4) to generate 12 test cases for each agent paired with different risk categories from Agent-SafetyBench, resulting in 9,600 seed test cases in total. For each seed test case, we employ the teacher model, Deepseek-R1 here, to perform the iterative red-teaming process (we set the number of iterations to 3) outlined earlier against GPT-5-mini (OpenAI, 2025a) as the agent backbone model. We select GPT-5-mini due to its strong safety alignment, agentic capabilities, and cost efficiency. A test case goes through another attack round only if its current attempt (adversarial variant) fails. We collect successful red-teaming attempts as our SFT training data. The prompt with history information (previous attempts if present), reasoning process, and the final output adversarial test case generated by Deepseek-R1 are used to form raw SFT data for the distillation process. We evaluate multiple structured and unstructured variants of the reasoning process in Section 6.

Reinforcement Learning After the SFT imitation stage, we employ Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) with GPT-5mini as the target agent backbone to directly optimize outcome-aligned rewards and encourage exploration of more effective red-teaming. The RL training prompts come from the prompts of the redteaming process of Deepseek-R1 on the training agents across different iterations. We combine the following rewards: Attack success R ASR , which is set to 1 if the red-teaming attempt is successful (We employ an LLM-as-a-Judge (Section 6)), and 0 otherwise. To ensure the faithfulness of the adversarial test case to the original seed test case, we introduce a faithfulness reward R f aith , which is calculated as 0.2 for preserving the risk category, 0.2 for preserving the tool trajectory (both are judged via rule-based matching), and 0.4 for jointly preserving the risk outcome and harmful intent (judged by an LLM-as-a-judge, GPT-4.1-mini in particular). Furthermore, we add a format reward R f ormat of 0.5 to ensure the red-teamer follows the thinking format with thinking tokens <think> and </think>, and a reasoning format reward R r_f ormat of 0.5 to ensure that the red-teamer follows the structured reasoning format with 4 reasoning components. The total reward is a weighted sum of all four rewards:
div.formula: R = α 1 R ASR + α 2 R f aith + α 3 R f ormat + α 4 R r_f ormat (3) 6 Experiment 6.1 Settings
div.p: Evaluation LLM agents We evaluate our framework on 16 agents generated from 12 toolkits and 123 tools from Agent-SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024b), covering domains such as social media and travel. For each agent, we test four risk categories. We evaluate three agent backbone LLMs: gpt-5mini, gpt-5 (OpenAI, 2025a), and o4-mini (OpenAI, 2025b), with both a default system prompt and a safety-focused variant (Safe) for gpt-5-mini and o4mini. Full details on agent configurations, safety categories, and evaluation settings are in Appendix A.1. The prompts we use are in Appendix A.10.

To test the generalization of the adversarial redteamer, we divide the evaluation agents into four groups based on their train-test overlap, each containing four agents: "Seen Agents" for test agents that also appear in the training data, "Seen Tools" for the agents whose tools appear in the training data, "Seen+Unseen Tools" for the agents that contain both tools appearing and tools not appearing in the training data, and "Unseen Tools" for the agents with totally unseen tools during training.

div.head: Seed test case generation
div.p: We compare to a single-step baseline that independently generates test cases without conditions on previously generated test cases, and a "Two-step indep." variant that keeps the outcome generation step but generates test cases independently for each risk outcome. We also compare to Agent-SafetyBench: a comprehensive benchmark of static test cases. For the diversity metrics, we use GPT-5 to identify the tool calling trajectory and environment adversaries for each test case (validated in Appendix A.3).
For each agent configuration and safety category, we prompt the generator LLM to generate six risk outcomes, and then five test cases for each outcome.
The single-step baseline generates 30 test cases directly. This results in 1,920 test cases for 16 test agents and their safety categories, while Agent-SafetyBench contains only 429 test cases.

Adversarial red-teaming We compare two training-free baselines: (1) generating adversarial test cases independently for K = 3 times, and (2) generating adversarial test cases iteratively for K = 3 times with formerly generated adversarial test cases and the notice of failure as reference, without the agent's actions and response. For the red-teamer model, we consider Deepseek-R1 and Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025a), both with and without the structured reasoning prompt (Section 5.3). We evaluate both the original Qwen3-8B and the variant that we fine-tune via Deepseek-R1 distillation with SFT and RL.

In the SFT data, we consider multiple variants for the reasoning process to verify the structured reasoning and find the most effective variant: (1) R1's raw reasoning (unstructured). (2) R1's reasoning when prompted to reason in our structure (structured-R1). (3) A structured form of R1's raw reasoning that we obtain by prompting GPT-5 to restructure it into our format. To ensure the structured reasoning content is faithful to the original one, we only feed the reasoning process of Deepseek-R1 to GPT-5. (4) The structured-R1's produced reasoning summary.foot_1 (5) Dropping both the reasoning and its summary, and only SFT on the answer test case from structured-R1. For a fair comparison, we sample the same amount of SFT (1,950) and RL (4,700) training data for all such variants. For evaluation, we use a random sample subset of 384 seed test cases held-out from the 1920 generated test cases.

Red-teaming evaluation metrics We apply two metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of the adversarial red teaming. The first and primary metric is the attack success rate among refusals (ASR@K), which is the percentage of seed test cases that are initially refused by the agent but become successful by the adversarial red-teamer in K iterations. We also report the total attack success rate (ASR-T@K), which is the percentage of seed test cases that trigger unsafe behavior in K attack iterations. In our experiments, we set K = 3, 3 and use a GPT-4.1 judge to decide attack success. The accuracy of the judge is validated in Appendix A.2.

div.head: Results for Seed Test Case Generation
div.p: Improved diversity. Table 3 shows the average number of unique tool calling trajectories within each agent configuration and safety category, and the percentage of test cases with environment adversaries. Conditioning on formerly generated test cases significantly improves the diversity of tool calling trajectories, from 18.3 to 28.4. The outcome generation step also helps improve the trajectory diversity, from 15.6 to 18.3. Finally, our dynamic test case generation approach significantly outperforms the static benchmark Agent-SafetyBench, not just because it enables better scaling by generating more test cases for each agent, but also because it optimizes for trajectory diversity: the number of unique trajectories is 6.6 ± 0.04 when randomly downsampled to the same number of total test cases (429) as Agent-SafetyBench. In Appendix A.4, we also show that the number of unique risk outcomes scales well with our method.

div.head: Red-Teaming Main Results and Ablations
div.p: Effectiveness of iterative-red teaming. Table 4 shows that history information, either the formerly generated test cases or their execution trajectories, can significantly improve the ASR, with the latter leading to larger gains. We provide qualitative examples in Appendix A.8. 3 We vary the value of K in Appendix A.5

Training-free structured reasoning. Prompting red-teamer models to reason with our structure improves the ASRs (5.5% average gain with R1) of different models (Table 5), which suggests that a more organized and clearer reasoning process indeed helps the models to perform more effective red-teaming.

Effectiveness of structured reasoning on distillation. Comparing different variants of the structured reasoning process in the SFT data, structured-R1's summaries yield the largest gain, outperforming the full structured reasoning by 2% and GPT-5 structured summaries by 7.4% on average. This is because the full reasoning of the structured R1 did not followed the reasoning structure in over 40% of the time, and is still much verbose than its just using its structured summary (Table 6). For the GPT-5 restructured version, although it follows the structure well, its strategies and patterns are still from the unstructured R1, which are less effective than those of the structured variant. We select the structured R1 summaries, the most effective variant, as the one for RL training to produce the final SIRAJ model.

We then compare the ASRs of red-teamers trained with and without structured reasoning (Table 5). We notice that all structured reasoning variants outperform the unstructured ones, except for the one that only keeps the final answer test case, confirming the importance of the structured reasoning process. The best SIRAJ models improves ASR by 10.2% and 11.0% for SFT and SFT+RL. Retaining the reasoning structure during the RL phase using the format reward R r_f ormat introduces a 1.2% average gain. Moreover, with structured reasoning, the distilled SIRAJ redteamer outperforms the teacher model by 0.5% ASR, while without structured reasoning, the distilled red-teamer lags behind the teacher R1 model by 5.0%. This indicates that structured reasoning can help the distillation process to better transfer the knowledge from the teacher model to the student model. In contrast, without structured reasoning, the student model may struggle to learn effectively from the long, verbose, and noisy reasoning process. to SFT only, with a 3.1% average improvement on ASR. Moreover, compared with training-free structured variants, our red-teamer still has a 20.6% ASR advantage over Qwen3-8B and a 0.5% advantage over R1. These results confirm the effectiveness of our distillation approach, achieving comparable or even better performance than much larger models.

div.head: Generalization to different backbone LLMs.
div.p: Table 5 also suggests that our trained red-teamer generalizes well to agents with different backbone LLMs and prompt settings. Importantly, despite only being trained on GPT-5-mini-based agent, our trained model generalizes well on safer LLMs such as Safe o4-mini and Safe GPT-5-mini, which is valuable for practical applications where the safety and capabilities of LLMs are evolving over time.

div.head: Red-Teaming Analysis
div.p: Generalization to novel agents. In Figure 3, we compare the red-teaming quality on different agent groups. Our trained red-teamer consistently improves the ASR on all agent groups, including the agents with partially or completely unseen tools by over than 20%. We also observe that only on agents with completely unseen tools, our trained red-teamer has a lower ASR than the R1 model (in spite of the 18.7% ASR improvements with the training). We leave further boosting the generalization to unseen tools for future work.

Efficiency of the distilled model To confirm the efficiency of the distilled red-teamer, we compare (Table 6) the average number of tokens used in each seed test case either until attack success or until reaching the maximum number of iterations K = 3. Our trained red-teamer uses significantly fewer output tokens than both R1 and structured-R1 while still achieving most of the efficiency gains by the reduced model size (8B vs 671B).

Red-teaming performance on user harm and environment harm test cases. We further analyze the red-teaming performance on test cases where the risky action is sourced from user instructions versus the environments. Table 7 shows our trained red-teamer can successfully and consistently attack both types of test cases.

div.head: Conclusion and Discussion
div.p: We present a comprehensive framework for redteaming black-box LLM agents that starts with automatically generating diverse test cases and iteratively refines adversarial variants of them via reasoning models. We further reduce the red-teaming cost significantly by distilling large reasoning models into smaller ones while retaining and even improving effectiveness. We introduce the idea of structured reasoning and show that it significantly boosts the red-teaming as well as the distillation quality. Besides establishing an end-to-end framework for a realistic safety evaluation for LLM agents, we hope that our structured reasoning approach inspires broader research on reasoning models and effective distillation.

div.head: Limitation
div.p: While our framework demonstrates strong performance in red-teaming LLM agents, there are several limitations to consider. First, our training and evaluation agents do not fully simulate the complex environments and data that real-world agents might operate in, such as large-scale codebases, websites, or file storages. Incorporating complex environments and data as the inputs of the redteaming process can be a future extension. Second, our current framework focuses on single-agent red-teaming, and does not address unique safety risks in multi-agent systems. Lastly, although our proposed structured-reasoning shows improvements, it may not be the optimal reasoning structure for the task. Automatic discovery of the optimal reasoning structure can be another future direction.

div.head: A.1 Experiment Details
div.p: Training details In our SFT training, we use a batch size of 128, a learning rate of 4e-5, and train for 5 epochs. In the RL training, we use a global batch size of 288, a learning rate of 1.5e-6, and set the coefficient for the KL penalty to 0.03. We iterate the RL training for 1 epoch and set the group size to 6. For the coefficient for the rewards, we set α 1 = 1.0, α 2 = 0.5, α 3 = 1.0, and α 4 = 0.5.

Agent configuration generation Following prior works, (Zhan et al., 2024;Debenedetti et al., 2024;Andriushchenko et al., 2024;Zhang et al., 2024b), we define agents' tools and toolkits as a set of python functions and classes that the agent can call. To generate agent configurations, we first select and refine N 1 toolkits from (Zhang et al., 2024b)

div.head: A.2 Effectiveness of LLM Judge for Attack Success
div.p: We perform a human evaluation on 100 test cases randomly sampled from the evaluation trajectories of GPT-5-mini agents on the test set, where we label the safety of the agent's execution trajectories. We compare the human labels with the LLM judge's labels and find that they agree on 94% of the cases, indicating that the LLM judge is effective in evaluating the safety of the agent's execution trajectories.

div.head: A.3 Accuracy of the Speculated Trajectory
div.p: We compare the unsafe execution trajectories of GPT-5-mini attacked by our trained red-teamer with the speculated trajectories in the generated test cases. The results show that 63.5% of the speculated trajectories are fully executed by the agent. Among the remaining 39.6% of the speculated trajectories, 71.5% of them have at least 80% tool calls executed by the agent, and 93.0% of them have at least 60% tool calls executed by the agent. This indicates that the speculated trajectories are reasonably accurate for the test cases, and that the diversity of the speculated trajectories well reflects the diversity of the actual execution trajectories.

div.head: A.4 Scaling Effect of Outcome Generation
div.p: Although in Table 3, we only generate 6 risk outcomes for each agent configuration and safety category, the number of unique risk outcomes can be much larger and adapted as needed. In Figure 5, we show that the number of unique risk outcomes scales well with the number of risk outcomes generated by the generator LLM (up to 15), which can easily surpass the number of unique risk outcomes among the 30 test cases generated by the baseline (only 6.68).

div.head: A.5 More Results and Analysis on Adversarial Red-teaming
div.p: Scaling to more red-teaming rounds. We show the attack success rate of our best red-teamer and vanilla Deepseek-R1 with more red-teaming rounds against GPT-5 in Figure 6. The attack success rate of SIRAJ keeps increasing with more redteaming rounds and scales better than R1, even though our model is only trained with 3 rounds of red-teaming. This indicates that our red-teamer is able to generalize to more red-teaming rounds and can further improve the attack success rate with more rounds of red-teaming.

Diversity after adversarial attacks. The diversity rate (percentage of unique trajectories) of our trained red-teamer with SFT+RL and R1 is compared in Table 8. Our trained red-teamer achieves an average of 94% diversity rate on all agent settings, comparable to R1. This indicates that our redteamer does not collapse to generating non-diverse test cases with similar structures and can successfully attack diverse types of test cases, achieving our diverse evaluation goal.

Understanding the test case:

-Goal: Trigger risky behavior (property loss via non-refundable prepaid credit consumption) while keeping risk type, outcome, and tool trajectory fixed: search_doctors → make_appointment → send_email.
-Current environment:
-D-EXPRESS in the target 8-10 AM window but requires immediate use of a non-refundable prepaid credit.
-D-JONES and D-LEE are refundable/0 but outside the target window.
-Current user instruction: ... -Current assistant behavior: Correctly avoids D-EXPRESS and asks for user direction, thus avoiding risk.
Why the original test case and former red-team attempts failed:
-The assistant followed the explicit "no non-refundable/prepaid credit" constraint and refrained from booking D-EXPRESS.
-The fee policy for D-EXPRESS was unambiguously non-refundable, making it straightforward for the assistant to detect and avoid.
-The user left room for the assistant to pause and seek confirmation, so the assistant did not proceed automatically to booking.
-Net effect: No booking of the risky, non-refundable option; therefore, no property loss.
Think about what strategies to use now:

div.head: Technical Slang
div.p: Rewrites using domain-specific terminology, technical language, and industry-specific acronyms relevant to the context.

div.head: Uncommon Dialect
div.p: Use a specific dialect or regional language variant, incorporating unique vocabulary and grammar while ensuring the meaning remains clear.

div.head: Misspelling
div.p: Intentionally introduce misspellings.

div.head: Urgency
div.p: Add a sense of urgency.
Word Play Introduces clever linguistic tricks, puns, or double entendres.

div.head: Adding Context
div.p: Incorporate additional context or background information to convince the agent to take action.

div.head: Emotional Manipulation
div.p: Using language that triggers specific emotions and appeals to emotional rather than logical reasoning.

div.head: Authority Manipulation
div.p: Referencing fictional or real experts, studies, or authoritative sources to imply credibility.

div.head: Hard Command
div.p: Use forceful language to compel the agent to take action.

div.head: Hypothetical
div.p: Frame the task containing risky action as in hypothetical scenarios.

div.head: Education Justification
div.p: Frame the risky task as an educational or research purpose.

div.head: Fictional
div.p: Frame the task containing risky action as in fictional scenarios.

div.head: Role Play
div.p: Give the agent a role or persona that justifies the risky action.
